newsitem.title: UK: British junior minister criticised in sleaze probe.
newsitem.headline: British junior minister criticised in sleaze probe.

text.p: A report into the conduct of a junior minister alleged to have tried to influence a parliamentary probe into sleaze in the ruling Conservative party is critical and hard hitting, the BBC said on Tuesday.
But the unanimous report by an all-party committee did not recommend Paymaster General David Willetts be suspended from parliament, it added.

"They are critical of the evidence given to them by David Willetts over his conduct of a whip (party manager) but they are not recommending his suspension from the house," the British Broadcasting Corporation said. "The official report is direct and hard hitting and may make it very hard for him to survive as a minister."

The Commons Committee on Standards and Privileges announced that it had concluded its report on Tuesday but chairman Tony Newton said none of the committee would comment on it before it was published on Wednesday.
With an election due by next May, the case will cause more damage to Prime Minister John Major and his Conservatives who are trailing badly behind the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls.

It will yet be another blow to Major, already battling Euro-sceptics in his party, who lost his parliamentary majority last week when a party member, who was angered by the closure of a local hospital, said he could no longer support the government.
Willetts has denied trying to influence the parliamentary probe into former trade minister Neil Hamilton who was alleged to have taken money in exchange for asking questions in parliament.
The committee investigated whether Willetts breached parliament's rules by interfering with Sir Geoffrey Johnson-Smith's handling of the affair, proposing to either rush it through or delay it.
In a memo to parliament's Standards and Privileges Committee, Willetts said there was nothing improper about a conversation he had when he was a whip in October 1994 with Johnson-Smith.
"I regret if my note, written in my first full week or work as a whip, should have inadvertently led to any confusion or misconception as to what acutally occurred," Willetts said.
Johnson-Smith also denied being influenced by Willetts.
The inquiry was demanded by opposition politicians after newspaper reports suggested that Willetts tried to get the inquiry into the "cash-for-questions" scandal shelved.
